articles.title: In 1974, Phoenix built Deer Valley Airport's parallel runways with a tire-rubber membrane beside a full-depth asphalt control; 11 years later, upkeep fell by 90%
articles.summary: Discover how Phoenix's innovative runway designs at Deer Valley Airport, implemented in 1974, drastically reduced maintenance costs by 90%, using advanced pavement technology to combat soil expansion issues.
articles.body: Phoenix built two parallel runways at Deer Valley Airport in 1974 and used different pavement designs to deal with a problem of soil expansion and contraction because of changes in moisture content, with an 11-year assessment finding that maintenance had fallen by 90% after the new designs were introduced, while the runway that incorporated an asphalt-rubber membrane also recorded lower construction costs for materials. The project was documented by Russell Howard Schnormeier, who was an engineer with the City of Phoenix, in a 1986 paper published in Transportation Research Record, and described how the airport's subgrade contained swelling material that was capable of going through volume changes of 8% as moisture levels varied. The city tested two designs to control those changes by keeping moisture conditions in the soil beneath relatively stable. The comparison gave engineers an opportunity to examine how different pavement structures performed under similar conditions, and rather than relying only on surface appearance, the study recorded moisture conditions in the subgrade and compared the designs' construction costs and maintenance requirements.One runway used conventional asphalt; the other added a rubber membraneThe first runway design made use of full-depth asphaltic concrete that was laid directly on native soil, while the second placed an asphalt-rubber membrane between the aggregate base and the subgrade, with asphaltic concrete being laid over the aggregate base. Asphalt-rubber combines asphalt cement with ground tire rubber, and in pavement applications, the material can form a sealing layer that limits how moisture moves and helps protect the underlying structure.The Federal Highway Administration describes asphalt-rubber as a binder that is made by blending crumb rubber with asphalt cement, and the material can be used in chip seals and other pavement treatments, including stress-absorbing membranes, with its properties depending on the rubber content, mixing temperature, and processing method. Phoenix had begun experimenting with asphalt-rubber in the 1960s, and the airport project was part of the city's wider effort that assessed whether the material could reduce pavement deterioration and the expense of maintaining roads and other paved surfaces.The 11-year assessment recorded a 90% maintenance reductionPeriodic checks found that subgrade moisture remained 3% to 4% below the optimum moisture content under both runway designs over 11 years, as per Schnormeier's report, and the design that incorporated asphalt-rubber also saved approximately 10% on construction material costs. The report recorded that maintenance was reduced by 90% after the designs were introduced, and linked the earlier maintenance burden to volume changes in the subgrade, which had created problems before the new pavement designs were applied.The report discusses the maintenance reduction after the application of the two methods, but it does not establish that the rubber membrane alone accounted for the entire 90% decline, as both designs were part of the airport's approach to managing the underlying soil. A later Phoenix pavement study that was published in 1991 reviewed pavement applications that dated back to the 1960s and described the use of rubberized seals to limit cracking and extend pavement service life. The authors also noted that performance varied according to pavement condition, construction details and traffic. The Deer Valley project provided an extended field comparison of two runway designs that were built on swelling soil, and its reported results included stable subgrade moisture readings, lower material costs for the asphalt-rubber design, and a substantial reduction in maintenance after the new methods were introduced.You use AI every day. articles.title: A US scrap-metal dealer paid about $14,000 for a gold egg at an antiques market, hoping to melt it for profit; years later it was identified as a lost imperial Fabergé treasure reportedly worth up to $33 million
articles.summary: Sometimes history turns up in the least likely places.
articles.body: Sometimes history turns up in the least likely places. For one Midwest scrap-metal dealer, that moment came at an antiques market, where an ornate gold egg seemed to be little more than an opportunity to make a modest profit. Bought for about $14,000 with the intention of selling it for scrap, the object instead turned out to be one of the long-lost Imperial Easter eggs created by Carl Fabergé for the Russian imperial family, states a report by JCK online.From scrap metal to royal treasureAccording to the online report, the dealer had hoped to make a quick return on his purchase. The egg contained a Vacheron Constantin watch, making its gold and timepiece components potentially valuable even if the object itself held little historical significance.But finding a buyer proved unexpectedly difficult. With interest in the item dwindling, the dealer turned to the internet and searched for clues using the words “egg” and “Vacheron Constantin”. That search led him to an article about surviving Fabergé eggs, featuring an image that appeared strikingly similar to the object sitting in his possession, explains the online report.The discovery prompted an extraordinary journey to London, where he approached Kieran McCarthy, director of the renowned antiques dealer Wartski, with a photograph of the egg.A missing piece of imperial historyAs per the report, further examination established that the object was an Imperial Easter egg dating to 1887. It was commissioned by Russian Emperor Alexander III as an Easter gift for Empress Maria Feodorovna and was among a celebrated series of 50 Imperial eggs produced by Fabergé.Only 42 of the 50 are currently accounted for. Eight remain missing, although five are thought to have been destroyed. Three are believed to have escaped Russia, and this egg is one of them, claims the report.Its survival is particularly remarkable given the upheaval that followed the Russian Revolution, states the report. The imperial treasures were seized by the Bolsheviks, many of which were subsequently sold abroad. The egg eventually disappeared from the historical record before resurfacing decades later in an American antiques market, also claims the report.An extraordinary piece of craftsmanshipThe egg is more than a valuable curiosity. Its pedestal is decorated with coloured-gold garlands suspended from cabochon blue sapphires and topped with bows set with rose diamonds. Inside sits a ladies' Vacheron Constantin watch, featuring a white enamel dial and diamond-set gold hands, elaborates the report by JCK.Despite its long and uncertain journey, the piece remains in remarkably good condition, although several gemstones are missing.How it travelled from revolutionary Russia to a Midwest antiques market remains unknown. One possibility is that it passed through the hands of American collector Armand Hammer, who had extensive connections to Russia and was known for acquiring Russian treasures. From there, its provenance may have gradually disappeared as it moved through private collections and dealers, states the report.From a kitchen counter to millionsThe scale of the discovery became clear when McCarthy eventually travelled to the dealer's home. The priceless imperial treasure was reportedly sitting in his kitchen, beside a cupcake. The egg was subsequently reported to have sold to a private collector for as much as $33 million, although that figure has never been officially confirmed. The anonymous finder is nevertheless believed to have received a life-changing sum.The egg was later displayed at Wartski, marking its first public appearance in 112 years. After spending decades hidden in plain sight, the Imperial Easter egg had finally returned to the spotlight.Images Courtesy: istock and InstagramYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Michigan couple bought a 116-year-old, 1,000-pound refrigerator for $4,995 on Facebook Marketplace; after seven weeks, a $1,200 move and reinforced floors, the 7-foot-wide appliance became the center of their kitchen
articles.summary: A refrigerator bought on Facebook Marketplace has turned into a major home renovation project for a couple in Michigan, US.
articles.body: A refrigerator bought on Facebook Marketplace has turned into a major home renovation project for a couple in Michigan, US. Melani Heldt, 34, and her husband Adam paid $4,995 for an antique icebox manufactured in 1910, only to discover that getting the 1,000-pound appliance into their farmhouse would take seven weeks. The refrigerator, measuring seven feet in height and width, required specialist movers, reinforced floors, and alterations to the house before the family could begin using it.The couple eventually paid $1,200 to transport the appliance, far more than they had initially expected, according to People Magazine. Another $800 went towards getting it operational. However, despite the additional expenses and the work involved, they have kept the refrigerator and even given it a name: Freddy.The purchase was part of a much larger plan to renovate their home. Melani and Adam had relocated from Arizona to Michigan after buying an old farmhouse without visiting it beforehand. They wanted to rebuild parts of the property themselves, with their two sons growing up in a home they had helped improve.Their kitchen was the first room they decided to renovate. But while the couple had already removed the existing fittings, they struggled to find a refrigerator that suited the space. For nearly two months, the designated area remained empty. Their search eventually ended with an appliance that was more than a century old.Why the couple chose a refrigerator from 1910According to People magazine, Adam discovered the icebox while browsing Facebook Marketplace. The listing caught their attention because the appliance was unlike the refrigerators they had been considering.It was originally manufactured in 1910 but had undergone a professional conversion for use in a restaurant. The conversion had been completed a few years earlier, and the appliance was still working. The restaurant was closing, which is why it had been offered for sale.At first, the couple discussed the idea jokingly. But they soon began considering whether they could actually use the refrigerator at home.They travelled for an hour and a half to examine it and take measurements. The seller offered to hold it for them, giving them time to decide whether the purchase was practical.They eventually went ahead, although the price of the refrigerator was only the beginning of their expenses.The biggest challenge was getting it insideThe refrigerator's size and weight made ordinary household moving arrangements unsuitable. The couple approached movers experienced in transporting heavy equipment, including bank safes.They initially believed the job would cost a few hundred dollars. Instead, complications during transportation increased the bill to $1,200.One difficulty was that the appliance could not fit through the available doorways. Its refrigeration lines had to be disconnected and the compressor removed so that it could be taken out of the restaurant and brought into the farmhouse.Even after it reached their property, getting it into position remained difficult. The movers had to take it up the porch steps and manoeuvre it through the dining area. Adam also removed a door and its surrounding frame to create enough clearance.The moving team spent around three hours positioning the refrigerator inside the house. By then, seven weeks had passed since the couple purchased it.However, having the appliance indoors did not mean it was ready for use. The family still needed to make sure the old building could safely support its weight.Farmhouse needed additional supportThe refrigerator weighs more than 1,000 pounds, making its placement particularly important in a property built in the 1800s.The couple chose a corner close to the farmhouse's external foundation walls. There was a basement beneath the room, supported by an old stone foundation.To make the floor stronger, they installed metal beams beneath the floor joists. The additional support was intended to prevent the weight of the refrigerator from causing the floor to collapse.The appliance remained empty for approximately a month after being moved into the room. Melani was still trying to arrange the electrical and plumbing work required to get it running.Once it became operational, another issue emerged. Although the icebox had been converted into a refrigerator, it still required regular attention to its drainage system.The original appliance had used a large block of ice to cool its compartments. Following its conversion, a small pipe had been installed to drain water, but the couple had not connected it to their home's plumbing.For about a year, they have been collecting the water in a stainless steel bowl and emptying it every two or three days. They have even set reminders to make sure the container does not overflow.The couple intends to connect the drainage pipe to a pump in their basement, which would remove the need to empty the bowl manually.The antique appliance is now part of family lifeDespite the complications, the refrigerator is now being used to store the family's food. One of its compartments has been set aside for the couple's two sons, who use it for their drinks and snacks.Their unusual purchase has attracted interest from others considering similar appliances. Melani said some people had contacted her after finding antique refrigerators of their own, with several exploring the possibility of converting them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: US President Donald Trump drew laughter from guests at the White House on Monday after questioning whether first lady Melania Trump’s signature 'means anything' as the couple signed an executive order aimed at boosting research into women’s health.The exchange took place on Monday, during an event in the Rose Garden, where the president signed an order establishing a dedicated women’s health research division at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a White House task force to address gaps in medical research.As Melania reached for her “Be Best” pen to sign the document, Trump told the gathering, “I don’t know if her signature means anything.” The comment appeared to prompt awkward laughter among some guests gathered for the ceremony.The first lady replied, “Yours is the most important,” before continuing to sign the document.Melania had launched her “Be Best” initiative during Trump’s first presidential term. The programme focused on children’s well-being, online safety and the prevention of drug abuse.Trump later appeared to admire his wife’s signature as he compared it with his own.“Oh! That looks very similar!” he said with a smile.The new initiative was championed by Melania, who has called for greater investment in research into conditions affecting women. The order is intended to promote new research, improve diagnostic technologies and expand treatment options for diseases that have historically received insufficient attention.“Beginning today we will change the reality of women's health,” Melania said while outlining the initiative. “Previous generations fought for women's rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”Speaking after his wife, Trump said the order would “promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women”.White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Health and Human Services secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr will lead the White House task force, according to details of the initiative. Wiles has publicly discussed completing treatment for breast cancer.The announcement follows a series of meetings between the first lady and federal health officials on improving research and care for women.You use AI every day. articles.title: He was 9 when Neil Armstrong walked on the Moon; 57 years later, retired pilot Ken Schreiber has spent $400,000 to help preserve the astronaut's boyhood home and open it to visitors
articles.summary: In July 1969, Ken Schreiber was nine years old when Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon.
articles.body: In July 1969, Ken Schreiber was nine years old when Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon. The moment stayed with him, and like Armstrong, Schreiber eventually became a military fighter pilot. Fifty-seven years later, his admiration for the astronaut led him to donate $400,000 to help preserve the house where Armstrong spent part of his childhood.As reported by the Associated Press (AP), the donation enabled the Auglaize County Historical Society to acquire Armstrong's boyhood home in Wapakoneta, Ohio. The purchase was finalised on October 19, 2026. The society plans to restore the house to its appearance during Armstrong's childhood and hopes to open it for public tours by 2030, the centenary of his birth.Schreiber, a retired pilot who spent 20 years in the US Air Force before retiring from American Airlines, stepped in after learning that the property was for sale and that no one had come forward to preserve it. He also remembered his father's advice to “make a mark in life,” something he said had stayed with him.Why Schreiber decided to helpSchreiber grew up in Dayton, Ohio, about 60 miles south of Wapakoneta. He admired Armstrong for his achievements, modesty and character, according to the AP report. When he read in August 2026 that Armstrong's childhood home had gone on the market, he became concerned about what might happen to the property. The house was being offered for sale for the first time in nearly 40 years, and there had been no immediate effort to secure its future as a historic site.Schreiber initially asked friends to contribute towards buying the house. He eventually decided to donate the $400,000 himself, making it possible for the historical society to acquire the property. Despite growing up relatively close to Armstrong's hometown, Schreiber had never visited the Armstrong Air and Space Museum until the summer of 2026. He also toured the house.The house where Armstrong built model planesAccording to AP, The two-storey house at 601 W. Benton Street played an important role in Armstrong's early interest in aviation. His family bought the property in 1944, when he was a teenager, after moving several times because of his father's work. As per AP’s earlier report on the property, Armstrong built model aeroplanes using balsa wood and glue in the dining room. He tested them in a wind tunnel he had constructed in the basement.He also launched model planes from the rear window of his bedroom to see how far they would fly. The house was part of the environment in which he developed his interest in flight, years before he became an astronaut. Armstrong made his first solo flight and earned his pilot's licence at the age of 16. Two decades later, he travelled to the Moon as commander of Apollo 11, alongside Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. On July 20, 1969, Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface.The house remains largely similar in its exterior and internal layout, although it has been updated over the years. Armstrong's former bedroom now contains photographs and paintings related to the Moon landing, along with signed photographs of astronauts who have visited.The previous owner wanted to preserve its historyKaren Mikesell, a retired history teacher, bought the house in 1988. She worked to preserve its character and welcomed astronauts who wanted to see where Armstrong had grown up. According to the AP, Mikesell hosted nine astronauts over the years, including Buzz Aldrin, who visited Armstrong's former bedroom several years after Armstrong died in 2012. She believed the house had historical value beyond its connection to a famous astronaut and wanted it to remain a place that could inspire future generations. The house was never formally open to the public, although it became a stop for visitors to the nearby Armstrong Air and Space Museum who wanted to learn more about the astronaut's early life.Local leaders welcome the preservation effortThe purchase has also drawn support from the local community. As reported by American media house Hometown Stations, Wapakoneta Mayor Dan Lee described the house as a place where Armstrong's early dreams took shape. He also referred to Armstrong's early efforts to learn to fly, noting that he cycled to the airport to earn his pilot's licence before he could drive a car. Lee thanked Schreiber for supporting the preservation of the property, describing the donation as an investment in American history.When will the house open to visitors?The Auglaize County Historical Society plans to restore the property to reflect how it looked in the 1940s, when Armstrong lived there. The work will require further fundraising and research into the house's original appearance. The Wapakoneta Community Foundation has also established a fund to support the property's upkeep and restoration, according to Hometown Stations. Schreiber's donation has secured the property for the historical society, but restoration and maintenance will require additional support. The planned opening will depend on the work being completed and the funds being raised.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: France in flames: How student protests spiralled into nationwide unrest
articles.summary: What began as student protests over deteriorating school conditions has escalated into a nationwide crisis in France, with more than 2,000 arrests,
articles.body: What began as student protests over deteriorating school conditions has escalated into a nationwide crisis in France, with more than 2,000 arrests, thousands of businesses damaged or looted and public buildings set on fire. More than half a million people took part in demonstrations across the country on October 17, according to the interior ministry, as anger over underfunded public services and rising living costs brought students, workers, farmers and other groups onto the streets.The violence has raised three central questions: How did the protests spread so rapidly? Did authorities fail to anticipate the scale of the unrest? Did far-left groups exploit the demonstrations to fuel disorder? While the government has blamed far-left agitators and looters, opposition leaders have pointed to years of discontent over public services and economic pressures. President Emmanuel Macron has acknowledged failures in planning and intelligence, rejected the interior minister’s resignation and ordered a review of policing methods.How did student protests turn into nationwide unrest?The demonstrations began in September, when high school students blockaded schools to protest overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, deteriorating infrastructure and what they described as inadequate funding. Some also demanded changes to the state-run system used to determine university admissions, which they consider unfairly selective.The movement expanded in early October as teachers, parents, trade union members, farmers and other groups joined the demonstrations. Their demands extended beyond education to include rising living costs, fuel prices and declining public services, including healthcare, housing and welfare.Also read - France student protests: Why are thousands of students blocking schools and taking to the streets?The mobilisation culminated in nationwide marches on October 17. The interior ministry estimated that around 550,000 people participated, while the CGT trade union put the figure at more than 800,000.Although most demonstrations were peaceful, groups of rioters targeted shops, supermarkets, public buildings and police vehicles. Authorities said thousands of businesses were affected, while several municipal and government buildings suffered fires or other damage.In Limoges, a fire badly damaged the historic town hall, causing its roof to collapse. In Lyon, a tourist office was set ablaze, while authorities in Bordeaux reported an attack on the prefect's residence. Shops and businesses in Paris, Marseille and Lille were also targeted.The spread of violence across multiple cities transformed a protest movement rooted in public grievances into a nationwide law-and-order crisis. The scale of the destruction also intensified scrutiny of the authorities' ability to protect public property and prevent peaceful demonstrations from turning violent.How did intelligence failures and police deployment contribute?One of the central questions is why security forces were unable to prevent violence from spreading across several cities despite weeks of demonstrations.Interior minister Laurent Nuñez acknowledged that authorities had failed to anticipate the scale of the mobilisation and admitted that police had "lost control" in some major cities. He also said policing numbers had fallen short in certain areas.On Monday, Macron acknowledged “failures in anticipation and intelligence” but rejected Nuñez's resignation, which the interior minister had submitted on Sunday. The Élysée Palace said the president wanted the interior ministry to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence gathering that contributed to the violence. Macron also called for new operational methods for security forces.The movement of violent groups away from the main demonstrations appears to have complicated the police response. Fabien Jobard, a researcher at the French National Centre for Scientific Research, told TIME that rioters dispersed beyond the main protest areas, apparently catching police off guard.This movement left authorities with less time to deploy sufficient forces at different locations. With violence spreading across city centres, commercial districts and public buildings, police also faced the challenge of protecting multiple potential targets simultaneously.The unrest has revived questions about France's approach to crowd control. The country has experienced prolonged clashes during previous protest movements, including the Yellow Vest movement that began in 2018 over fuel taxes and broader economic grievances, and demonstrations against pension reforms in 2023.However, the available information does not establish that a single intelligence failure or policing decision caused the nationwide violence. The government's own admission points to shortcomings in anticipating the mobilisation, while the dispersal of rioters presented an additional operational challenge.How did ultra-left groups become part of the controversy?The government has accused far-left activists and organised groups of exploiting the demonstrations to provoke confrontation and undermine public order.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the authorities were dealing with a "shadowy network" of instigators and argued that some groups wanted to create widespread disorder ahead of next year's presidential election.Nuñez also blamed what he described as "hordes of troublemakers and looters" and "far-left activists", saying police tactics needed to adapt to highly mobile groups.The government's position is that the violence was not simply an extension of the student movement, but also involved people who used demonstrations as an opportunity to attack public property and loot businesses.The accusations have been contested by the political opposition. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, argued that the unrest reflected deeper problems with the government's handling of public services.Mélenchon described the protest movement as “the result of ten disastrous years in which President Macron has disorganized the state and public services.”The competing explanations point to two issues that need to be distinguished: why people joined the protests and who was responsible for the violence. Anger over schools, living costs and public spending helps explain the scale of the demonstrations, but it does not establish who organised or carried out individual attacks.The available evidence also does not establish that far-left groups orchestrated the entire unrest. The government's allegations remain central to the political dispute, while the extent of any organised role would need to be assessed through police investigations and evidence about specific incidents.How did economic anger fuel the protests?The unrest has unfolded against growing frustration over the cost of living and the condition of public services in France.Students have complained about overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and inadequate school infrastructure. Other groups have joined the movement over rising fuel prices, pressure on household budgets and concerns about access to healthcare, housing and welfare.Fuel costs have become another source of anger amid disruption to energy supplies linked to the war involving Iran. Farmers have also raised concerns about agricultural expenses.The demonstrations have consequently drawn support from groups with different demands, making the mobilisation broader than a conventional student protest. Organisers have described the movement as a convergence of education-related grievances and wider economic discontent.The government's fiscal position has added to the political pressure. France's high public debt and debate over spending have intensified scrutiny of its ability to fund public services while controlling government expenditure.Macron has acknowledged that young people's concerns need to be heard and said the government was working with fuel distributors to deliver a tangible impact on prices. However, the political dispute over public spending and the government's response has continued alongside the security crisis.Economic grievances help explain why the demonstrations attracted such a wide range of participants. They do not, on their own, explain why some gatherings turned violent, making it necessary to examine the conduct of rioters and the authorities' response separately.How are curfews helping the government restore order?Authorities have introduced local restrictions to prevent further violence and protect businesses following the weekend's destruction.Paris police imposed an overnight curfew covering Place de la République, where clashes took place, and the Les Halles shopping district. The restrictions were scheduled to run from 11pm on Monday until 6am on Tuesday, with gatherings and demonstrations also prohibited from 8pm.Other local authorities introduced restrictions, including overnight curfews for minors in parts of Lille and Nice. Bordeaux also announced a week-long night curfew for unaccompanied minors following violence and looting in the city centre.Also read - France unrest: PM orders curfews, hints at declaring emergency; over 2,400 arrestedLecornu said the government preferred limited, localised curfews rather than a nationwide measure and indicated that restrictions could be extended where necessary."The targeted curfews have contributed to the calm of last night," the prime minister said on X on Tuesday, adding that the measures could be extended "where the situation requires it".France's cities were reported to have remained calm overnight under the new restrictions, giving the government a temporary reprieve. But protest groups have announced further demonstrations, including calls for renewed student mobilisation and actions associated with the Yellow Vest movement over fuel costs.The government is therefore facing two parallel challenges: restoring public order and addressing the grievances that brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets. Curfews may help limit opportunities for further disorder, but they do not resolve the underlying disputes over education, living costs and public services.How has the unrest intensified political pressure on Macron?The unrest has triggered a wider political confrontation as France approaches its next presidential election, scheduled for 2027.Far-right National Rally leader Jordan Bardella accused the government of failing to protect the public, while Marine Le Pen called for calm and condemned the destruction.“Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a form of expression. And chaos cannot serve as a project for France,” Le Pen said in a video address.Macron has vowed that those responsible for looting and attacks on public buildings will be held accountable. Economy Minister Roland Lescure has also pledged support for businesses affected by the destruction.The government has faced criticism from both the right and the left, with opponents disputing its handling of the security situation and its broader economic and public-service policies.The coming days will test whether local curfews and revised police tactics can prevent another wave of violence. Further demonstrations could also reveal whether the movement remains focused on student grievances and living costs or becomes more closely associated with wider opposition to Macron's government.How did the protests spiral out of control?France's unrest cannot be explained by a single factor on the available evidence. Public anger over education, living costs and public services helped bring hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets. The alleged involvement of far-left activists and looters added another dimension, while the government's admission of failures in anticipation and intelligence raised questions about police preparedness.The key distinction is between the grievances that fuelled the mobilisation and the actions that turned parts of it violent. The available information does not establish that ultra-left groups orchestrated the nationwide unrest, nor does it show that soft policing alone caused the escalation.The crisis has exposed the challenge of responding to widespread public discontent while preventing violent groups from exploiting demonstrations. Whether the government can restore order will depend not only on policing and intelligence reforms, but also on how it addresses the wider grievances driving the protests.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fighter jets, warships and air defences: What Egypt could bring to Saudi Arabia's fight against the Houthis
articles.summary: Egypt is weighing military support for Saudi Arabia against Yemen's Houthis, a move that could bring one of the Middle East's largest militaries into the
articles.body: Egypt is weighing military support for Saudi Arabia against Yemen's Houthis, a move that could bring one of the Middle East's largest militaries into the escalating conflict, with implications for Red Sea security, the Suez Canal and the balance of power in the Arabian Peninsula. According to reports, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has sought parliamentary authorisation to provide military assistance to Riyadh if requested, and parliament has postponed its vote to October 26 amid questions about the mission's objectives, duration and cost. Sisi has described the role as defensive, and the proposal does not mean Egypt has decided to send ground troops into Yemen. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said on October 13 that Egypt would respond to whatever Saudi Arabia asks of it, and that Cairo was seriously considering joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.Egypt's interest goes beyond its ties with Riyadh. The Red Sea links the Suez Canal to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Houthi attacks on commercial vessels since November 2023 pushed shipping companies to go around the Cape of Good Hope. According to Associated Press reporting, canal revenue fell from a record $10.25 billion in 2023 to $3.991 billion in 2024. Saudi Arabia is also an important economic partner for Egypt through investment, financial support and jobs for Egyptian workers in the Gulf.History is a caution. Egypt intervened in Yemen in 1962 after army officers overthrew the monarchy, with President Gamal Abdel Nasser backing the republicans while Saudi Arabia supported the royalists. A limited deployment grew to around 50,000 troops within a year and about 70,000 by the summer of 1965, according to a study published by Cambridge University Press. Egyptian forces faced mountain terrain, tribal resistance and outside support for their opponents, and the campaign ended in 1967 after the defeat in the Six-Day War. Some assessments put Egyptian military deaths at about 26,000. Egypt later joined the Saudi-led coalition in March 2015 with naval and air forces, a far more limited role.Egypt has capabilities that could help. Its air force flies Rafale, F-16 and MiG-29M/M2 fighters and E-2C Hawkeye early-warning aircraft, which could support patrols, surveillance and detection of incoming threats. Its air defences include the S-300VM, Buk, Tor and Hawk systems, though nothing shows Cairo will transfer them, as it must also defend its own territory. The navy has frigates, corvettes, missile boats, submarines and Mistral-class helicopter carriers, and could escort merchant ships and monitor traffic in the Red Sea. Logistics and intelligence sharing are other possible contributions.The Houthis, formally Ansar Allah, are a different kind of opponent. They have ballistic and cruise missiles, one-way attack drones and reconnaissance drones, and they use mobile launchers and dispersal that make detection hard. Defending against them takes surveillance, early warning, communications and enough interceptors, and cheap drones can force defenders to spend costly missiles. Air defence help and naval patrols could strengthen the coalition, but they would not remove the Houthis' ability to attack or settle Yemen's internal divisions.The main questions are whether parliament approves, which assets are sent, and whether operations stay within Saudi territory and sea approaches or reach into Yemen. Cost, duration and command arrangements will also matter, and the 1960s campaign is the reference point.

articles.title: 'Dream come true’: IAF chief AP Singh flies last sortie in uniform in Kiran aircraft
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Indian Air Force (IAF) Chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh on Tuesday flew his “last sortie in uniform” in a Kiran aircraft at the Air Force
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Indian Air Force (IAF) Chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh on Tuesday flew his “last sortie in uniform” in a Kiran aircraft at the Air Force Academy (AFA) in Dundigal near Hyderabad, completing a full circle in his flying career alongside the instructor who taught him to fly four decades ago.According to news agency PTI, Singh flew with Wing Commander (retd) V S Kochchar, who trained him at the academy in 1984.Recalling his first flight on January 20, 1984, Singh said, “I started my journey with the same aircraft. I think I must be the only Chief who is retiring on the basic aircraft he flew is still serving.”Expressing gratitude to his former instructor, Singh said, “I am very grateful to my instructor Kochchar sir who taught me flying in the beginning, in this place itself. So, I just wanted the circle to be complete.”Singh was given a water cannon salute as he landed at the academy. He graduated from the AFA in 1984 with a Sword of Honour.The IAF chief had flown his last fighter jet sortie aboard the indigenous Tejas on October 12 during Exercise Tarang Shakti at Jodhpur Air Force Station. Tuesday's flight in the Kiran marked his last sortie in uniform, days before his expected retirement later this month.Kochchar, 73, described Singh as the “brightest pupil ever” and the “best chief”, adding that getting “one more trip” with his former student was a dream come true.

articles.title: Bhagwat warns protests can become political tools, urges restraint from govt too
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Warning that when a movement becomes “a tool of politics”, forces seeking to undermine India take advantage, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Tuesday
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Warning that when a movement becomes “a tool of politics”, forces seeking to undermine India take advantage, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Tuesday linked political protests and distrust of institutions to alleged foreign attempts to destabilise the country. But his Vijayadashami address in Nagpur also carried a message for governments: respect citizens' dignity, act within constitutional limits and avoid deepening divisions while addressing grievances.The remarks came amid protests over the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. Bhagwat did not name the Commission, SIR or any political party, nor did he present evidence connecting the protests with foreign forces.The warning was not new. In 2023, Bhagwat had identified “cultural Marxists” and “Woke” forces as promoting anarchy through education, media and public discourse. In 2024, he invoked the “Deep State”, alleging attempts to foster grievances and distrust of institutions. His 2025 Vijayadashami address warned against forces seeking to reproduce political upheavals witnessed in neighbouring countries.What's different this year was the emphasis: instead of naming ideological adversaries, Bhagwat described their alleged methods, from deepening disagreements and cultivating a sense of victimhood to undermining faith in national institutions and drawing domestic political actors into the process.Claiming that powers seeking to install proxies in other countries regarded India's rise as a threat, he said: “They devise plans and work towards finding ways to dismantle Bharat, Hindu society, and Sangh.” Some ambitious political leaders, driven by “petty political interests”, joined such efforts, he alleged, without identifying them.Yet Bhagwat acknowledged the legitimacy of grievances. “In our vast society problems do exist. There are likely to be numerous shortcomings in the system as well. It is only natural that these may lead to agitations,” he said. “However, such agitations should aim to provide solutions.”He applied that standard to protesters, political leaders and the state alike, asking them not to create “discord, animosity, resentment, bitterness, or divisions”. Even when emotions ran high, their actions should remain within the Constitution and law. He warned that “the lure of votes, cheap popularity, or political gains” must not overpower prudence and goodwill.Earlier in the address, he specifically urged government officials implementing campaigns and policies to be courteous and considerate, and to respect citizens' dignity. “Experience shows that it is neither the government alone that can resolve all the problems of society, nor is it true that problems can be resolved only through agitations,” he said, advocating dialogue and community participation.That theme opened into the RSS's post-centenary plans. Bhagwat said Swayamsevaks would work to bring together organisations combating drug addiction and build nationwide resistance to what he called a “serious national problem”. He also urged the government to consider restrictions on OTT platforms, while asking families to teach young people to distinguish appropriate from inappropriate digital content.Although concerns over drugs and digital content had figured in his 2024 address too, the proposed nationwide mobilisation gave the anti-drug initiative a more specific organisational direction.In education, he cited observations from around 1,296 rural schools across 210 districts in 21 Sangh organisational regions, claiming improvements in attendance, learning and parental involvement where Swayamsevaks and villagers cooperated. No underlying methodology was disclosed in the speech.Bhagwat said centenary outreach had covered over 10 crore households in 4.61 lakh villages and 41,076 urban localities. Contacts at home and abroad would continue, he indicated. The organisation's five initiatives — social harmony, family awareness, environment, self-awareness and Swadeshi, and civic discipline — were “not merely programs to be undertaken for a year”, but intended to change everyday conduct.On identity, Bhagwat said the Hindu worldview prescribed no particular form of worship, food habit, language or caste, and called for acceptance of diversity within shared national belonging. He also advocated singing 'Vande Mataram' in full, entering a dispute in which Congress has reaffirmed its decision to sing only the first two stanzas at party events.The address thus combined a familiar warning about alleged external interference with a stronger appeal for constitutional restraint and a continuing society-led role for the RSS beyond its centenary.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Kylie Jenner launched a lip kit in 2015 and built a global cosmetics brand; Coty agreed to pay $600 million for a 51% stake in 2019
articles.summary: Few beauty stories capture the power of social media as clearly as the rise of Kylie Jenner's cosmetics business.
articles.body: Few beauty stories capture the power of social media as clearly as the rise of Kylie Jenner's cosmetics business. What began in November 2015 as a debut lip kit became Kylie Cosmetics, a brand that built a devoted audience online and then attracted one of the largest beauty companies in the world. In November 2019, that company, Coty, agreed to buy a majority stake in the business for 600 million dollars. Here’s how the brand grew, what the agreement contained, why the numbers mattered, and how the partnership was designed to carry the business into new global markets.How the November 2015 Kylie Lip Kit launch became Kylie Cosmetics, a beauty brand with global reachCoty's press release describes the origin story plainly. In November 2015, Kylie Jenner launched Kylie Cosmetics, and the debut product, the Kylie Lip Kit, was a sell-out success. Her online store, KylieCosmetics.com, is one of the most successful online stores in the world, and the range grew well beyond lips to include eyeliners, eyeshadows, blushes, highlighters, concealers, brushes and makeup bags, plus limited edition sets released throughout the year. In May 2019, she introduced Kylie Skin, a range of skincare products. The audience behind it was enormous, Coty says she has more than 270 million followers across her personal and brand social media channels, and that both brands are among the fastest-growing and most-engaged beauty brands on social media. Forbes featured her as the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in August 2018.Why Coty agreed to pay 600 million dollars for 51 per cent ownership of the Kylie Jenner partnershipOn 18 November 2019, Coty and Kylie Jenner announced a long-term strategic partnership. Under the terms of the agreement, Coty would acquire 51 per cent ownership in the partnership for 600 million dollars, and the acquisition was expected to close in the third quarter of Coty's fiscal year 2020. Coty described the transaction as a key milestone in its ongoing transformation into a more focused and agile company. Chairman of the Board Peter Harf told the public that the partnership was an exciting step in Coty's renewed emphasis on its beauty business, calling Kylie Jenner a modern-day icon with an incredible sense of the beauty consumer. Pierre Laubies, Coty's chief executive officer, told the public the company was pleased to welcome her into its organisation and family.177 million dollars in revenue, growth targets and the financial case for CotyCoty's press release sets out the financial case in specific terms. Kylie Cosmetics generated an estimated 177 million dollars in net revenues over the preceding twelve months. Coty said it expected the transaction to add more than 1 per cent per year to the net revenue growth of its core fragrance, cosmetics and skin care portfolio over the next three years. The company also expected the deal to be neutral to its earnings per share in the first year and to add to them afterwards, and it expected the return on invested capital to exceed its cost of capital by fiscal year 2023. Tiger Shark served as an advisor to Coty on the transaction. Coty also scheduled a conference call that morning, with the live audio webcast and presentation slides made available through its investor relations website.How creative control, licensing and Coty's manufacturing reach shaped the global beauty expansion planThe agreement divides responsibilities along each side's strengths. Together, Coty and Kylie Jenner set and lead the strategic direction, focusing on global expansion and entry into new beauty categories. Kylie Jenner and her team keep leading all creative efforts in product and communications, building on her global reach through social media. Coty takes overall responsibility for developing the portfolio, drawing on its knowledge of research and development, manufacturing, distribution and commercial strategy, and it acts as licensee for skincare, fragrances and nail products. All beauty categories continue to be sold through leading luxury beauty retailers and owned digital channels. Both parties aim to build what Coty calls a high-growth, digitally native beauty brand. Kylie Jenner told the public the partnership lets her team stay focused on creating and developing each product while building an international beauty powerhouse.Where Coty stands today as a global beauty company and how the Kylie Jenner partnership fits its plansCoty's own investor relations website shows the scale of the company that Kylie Jenner partnered with. Founded in Paris in 1904, Coty describes itself as one of the world's largest beauty companies, with a portfolio spanning fragrance, colour cosmetics, and skin and body care. The site lists the company as second globally in both fragrances and mass colour cosmetics, with more than 60 brands and licenses, about 11,300 employees, seven manufacturing sites and sales in more than 120 countries. For fiscal 2026, it reports net revenues of 5.8 billion dollars, adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of 847 million dollars, and free cash flow of 348 million dollars. Pairing that infrastructure with a creator-led brand is what the partnership set out to do.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: BJP’s delimitation gambit: How it can isolate Congress, puncture opposition’s SIR unity
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Is the government planning a new delimitation push to puncture the Congress’s bid to unite the opposition with protests against SIR?
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Is the government planning a new delimitation push to puncture the Congress’s bid to unite the opposition with protests against SIR? Union parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju has refuelled buzz that Parliament may be called for a short session to take up the legislation while also signalling Congress’s isolation on the issue by rejecting its demands for all-party consultations.The government had tried to push through a Constitution Amendment Bill in April this year in Lok Sabha but failed. The proposed legislation, which aimed at implementing 33% reservation for women in legislatures from 2029 and increasing the number of Lok Sabha seats to 850 did not get the mandatory two-thirds majority. The bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against. It needed support of at least 352 out of the 528 members who were present and voted.The Monsoon Session of Parliament was adjourned sine die on August 13, 2026. It has been 68 days since then. However, the session is yet to be prorogued. This gap has broken the previous record of a 28-day delay for the Monsoon Session in 2015 and has left the opposition, especially the Congress, worried.The Congress fears the government has been engaging in backroom moves with other parties in the opposition camp to cobble up a two-thirds majority and get the two Bills passed.Kharge's missives to PM ModiAn anxious Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge has written four letters to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the last one four days ago. The Congress has been trying to pre-empt a sudden, surprise push by the government to pass the delimitation and women’s reservation bills."You may kindly recall that I had first written to you on April 11, 2026, to convene an All-Party meeting before bringing any Constitutional Amendment Bill on Delimitation. You did not do so. Thereafter, you made the Bills public on the late evening of April 14, 2026 and convened a special session on April 16, 2026. The Constitutional Amendment Bill on Delimitation failed to muster the necessary two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha on April 17, 2026, by a decisive margin," said Kharge in his letter."Thereafter, on July 16, 2026 and August 27, 2026, I wrote to you again, repeating our request for an All-Party meeting. I am now doing so for a fourth time," the Congress chief said.Kharge cautioned the government against taking a unilateral approach on major constitutional reforms such as national delimitation, which directly affects parliamentary constituency boundaries and regional representation.Rijiju's sharp response to KhargeIn a sharp response to Kharge's Oct 16 letter to the Prime Minister, Rijiju said, "When after repeated requests Congress didn't give dates for discussion, govt's outreach extended to other political parties. Consultations were held with representatives of parties including SP, DMK, YSRCP, NCP (SP), Shiv Sena (UBT), AIMIM and BJD with a view to building a broader consensus in support of the proposed legislation."Rijiju also rejected Kharge’s concerns over the “unprecedented” delay in proroguing the Monsoon session. Dismissing Kharge’s contention, Rijiju cited precedents and underlined that no constitutional requirement existed prescribing a specific period within which a House must be prorogued following its adjournment sine die."The mere fact that a House has not been prorogued does not, by itself, give rise to any constitutional or procedural impropriety or irregularity," Rijiju said.Why are opposition parties worriedWhen Parliament is adjourned sine die and not prorogued, it can be convened for a session at short notice. Sine die adjournment means that the session is suspended indefinitely without setting a day for reconvening. It does not mean a formal end of the session, which requires an official prorogation order by the President of India. There is no specific timeframe for prorogation of Parliament after a session has been adjourned sine die. But normally this happens within a few days.Since the Delimitation Bill is a Constitution Amendment Bill and cannot be taken through an ordinance route it makes sense for the government to keep the option alive by not proroguing the session.For the opposition, this is a clear signal that the government is still trying to get the numbers. And that brings us to the second question of opposition unity.The SIR unity vs Delimitation dilemmaThe last few weeks have seen the opposition at its united best. The protests against SIR has seen the Congress not just reach out to but also accommodate every opposition party. There have been differences and some reports of one-upmanship, but by and large all parties have been together under the INDIA bloc. The DMK and AAP despite staying away from the opposition coalition’s prorgrammes are united in the cause. In fact, the DMK has sent mixed signals - supporting the agitation against NEET but also accusing the Congress of duplicity citing its support to VIjay and the TVK government in Tamil Nadu. The AAP, on the other hand, has been active with the Cockroach Janata Party and has actively joined their protest programmes. Then there are parties which have been on both sides, like the Shiv Sena (UBT), Mamata Banerjee.In fact, Naveen Patnaik’s Biju Janata Dal of Odisha that normally keeps equal distance from both the NDA and the INDIA bloc also joined one of the protests in Delhi to show solidarity with the cause.And it's not just political parties; several civil society groups have also joined the INDIA bloc platform, amplifying the demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the reversal of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which has led to huge deletions of voters in several poll-bound states.Interestingly, many political parties named by Kiren Rijiju in his statement have been part of the ongoing protests against SIR under the INDIA bloc. Some that haven’t joined the common protest have expressed solidarity with the cause and have protested separately.This clearly poses a challenge to opposition unity. The Congress and many other opposition parties have been against the SIR and also the Delimitation Bill. However, while many of them are with the Congress on the issue of SIR, their independent negotiations with the government on the Delimitation Bill will keep the grand-old-party worried.The BJP has reached out to several regional parties with an assurance that the proposed delimitation bill will not change the representation of states in Parliament, as the seats in Lok Sabha will be increased 50% across the states and not in proportion to the existing population as it should normally be under the delimitation process.The BJP-led NDA government’s move to tag the women’s reservation bill, which proposes to increase their representation in Lok Sabha, comes as an added pressure as well as incentive. If the parties oppose, they are labelled as anti-women by the BJP and its ruling allies in their respective states. On the other hand, if they accept the proposal, they get the benefit of accommodating additional women without impacting the existing dominance of men.Keen political contestClearly, this is going to be a keen contest between the BJP and the Congress. It will be interesting to see how the Congress manages to persuade its allies to stay united against BJP’s Delimitation plans. If some regional parties like the DMK, which are very unhappy with the Congress do decide to back the delimitation bill, will it take the sting out of the present SIR campaign?The Congress, anyways, needs to realise that SIR cannot be the only glue that will hold together the opposition parties. The Supreme Court is already hearing a clutch of SIR related petitions. Also, the Election Commission has started the process re-enrolment of voters and also of SSR, the Special Summary revision of electoral rolls, in 14 states and 3 Union Territories. So, SIR as a unifying bond may not help the Congress for long. The main opposition party needs to find lasting ways of ensuring that all its allies are united against the government.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Deeply regrettable’: Sanjay Raut’s Albania arson post draws flak from party colleague, others
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Rajya Sabha member and Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Priyanka Chaturvedi on Tuesday disagreed with her party colleague Sanjay Raut for
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Rajya Sabha member and Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Priyanka Chaturvedi on Tuesday disagreed with her party colleague Sanjay Raut for suggesting that India should learn a lesson from the student-led protests in Albania, which turned violent and targeted democratic institutions.Raut had claimed that people in Albania had set the country's Supreme Court ablaze for allegedly helping “corrupt prime ministers”.“The people of Albania have burned down the Supreme Court. The people were enraged because the Supreme Court was helping corrupt prime ministers. The protesting public has also attacked Parliament and government offices, as well as the ministers' homes,” Raut said in a post on X.“All countries should learn a lesson from these events. Especially India,” he added.Chaturvedi, however, condemned the remarks, saying India did not need to learn from any other country. She also warned against people taking the law into their own hands and destabilising institutions.“India does not need to learn from any other country. Albania is a small nation that endured years under a communist dictatorship; the idea that people should take the law into their own hands, disrupt order, and destabilise institutions, whether it be the Supreme Court or Parliament, is entirely unacceptable,” Chaturvedi said.“Those who suggest that we should draw inspiration from the protests in Bangladesh to pursue a regime change: this is deeply regrettable, as those protests were not merely led by students; they were eventually co-opted by an Islamist movement, which led to attacks on minorities, including Hindu minorities. Such violent regime change has no place in any democracy, and we should not look to examples like Albania, Paris, or other such instances for guidance,” she added.BJP also slammed Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut for his remarks.In a post in Marathi on X, Raut on Monday shared a 13-second video clip of a purported incident of arson in Albania, saying all countries should take a lesson from these events, "especially" India. The Shiv Sena (UBT) leader referred to India with an emoji of its national flag, instead of naming the country in his post.Reacting sharply to Raut's remark, BJP spokesperson Sidharth Yadav said, "The opposition leaders sometimes speak of bringing about a 'regime change' in India. At times, they suggest that Bangladesh has shown us the way.""And now, Sanjay Raut's remark that India should learn from Albania, where the Supreme Court was set on fire amidst widespread anarchy on the streets," he said in a video message, adding, "The opposition leaders in India seek to push the nation's democracy toward anarchy; nothing could be more unfortunate than this."This comes amid widespread protests in Albania, with demonstrators demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.Protesters have targeted government buildings and set fires at several locations, including parts of the Supreme Court.Led by students, the demonstrations have been fuelled by public anger over alleged corruption, unemployment and poor education standards.Police said 388 people had been charged with criminal offences linked to the protests. Several police officers and demonstrators have also been injured.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
